#663. Inside the ‘Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic’: A Recipe for Blending Brands With TV (and a Full-Circle Career Moment for Host Drew Barrymore)

The folks behind CBS‘ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic are hoping to make this holiday special an annual Thanksgiving week tradition.

“I feel like this is going to become part of our cultural tradition,” says Scott Weintrob, founder of Studio Large Eyes and executive producer of the special. “Every Thanksgiving for the next 10 years, with the Pillsbury Bake-Off as the trigger to Thanksgiving week.”

The show is actually a collaboration between CBS and General Mills — which, incidentally, owns the “Bake-Off” trademark in the United States. (“Which is why they cannot call The Great British Bake Off the Bake Off in the U.S. and they have to call it The Great British Baking Show,” says Lisa Balzo, head of brand studio partnerships at General Mills.) Related Stories TV 'Survivor 51' Star Lewis Kelly on His $1 Million Coin Flip and Joining the Cast at the Last Minute TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors

In developing the special, Weintrob drew on his background in advertising, which has included award-winning work with Rihanna (he designed and directed Amazon’s Emmy-winning Savage x Fenty show) along with Lewis Hamilton x Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, reimagining the film’s classic valet scene with Lewis Hamilton, Edward Norton and Ferrari, which went viral. (He also recently directed and produced Mr. T: I Pity the Fool for Netflix and created Orlando Bloom: To the Edge for Peacock.)

Weintrob’s company, Studio Large Eyes, aims to create brand-inspired entertainment with the philosophy “entertainment first, marketing second.” He says his background crossing both advertising and TV gives him a unique perspective to understand both parties and what their objectives are. “They are quite different,” he says. “And they have different approaches. Being able to talk to networks and streamers and also being able to talk to global brands. I had this in-between knowledge because they are different in so many ways but they all are trying to do the same thing, so I was perfectly positioned to be the conduit.”

Balzo notes that GM, parent company of Pillsbury, had been interested in the idea of a “big grand spectacle” that would incorporate one of the company’s brands. She had already met Weintrob previously at an industry event, and the two began having conversations about some options. “I started talking [with Weintrob] about the history of the Bake-Off, and how it used to be this kind of big grand spectacle that was put on as a live event,” she says. “Over the years, we’ve done various different things with it, and it’s become a smaller digital activation. We’ve also collaborated with the Food Network. I mentioned to Scott that we have been talking about, for years, wanting to bring it back to its full glory. And he pitched this incredible live event.”

“What I originally said to them was, I love the format of the Westminster Dog Show as a baking show, a large event as a live, two-hour special focusing on ordinary people doing extraordinary things,” Weintrob recalls. They agreed on the idea and decided that Thanksgiving would be a key time for the project to air. “I felt we had the opportunity to go and talk to distributors about making this wonderful event. And that’s the key word: It’s an event.”

Balzo says the concept “felt so perfect” and “felt very serendipitous to me at the time. He had this project in his head that that was so perfectly aligned with Pillsbury and what we were looking to do with the Bake Off.”

Back to that trademark: Pillsbury held its first Bake-Off in 1949, when it was called Pillsbury’s Best Grand National Baking Contest. A total of 100 finalists went to New York to compete, and each received at least $100 and kept the G.E. stove they baked on. Eleanor Roosevelt presented the grand prizes, which ranged from $25,000 to $50,000.

Balzo says that baking competitions are immensely watchable because it offers inspiration for viewers at home. “The recipes they’re making are so relatable, and I think people are really going to feel that when they’re watching” the new show, she said, adding that many brands are trying to get into this space, and for GM, the Bake-Off special offers an “authentic connection” with Pillsbury. “It feels like bringing back something that people have already experienced and want more of, as opposed to trying to advertise through content like this.”

For 2026’s Bake-Off, Weintrob began assembling a production team and then setting up meetings with distributors. “When network TV is involved, the word ‘spectacle’ is a brilliant word as a reference point,” he shares. “It needs to be a spectacle to work on network, and CBS saw just how great the show could be. They were the perfect partner to work with.”

Balzo agrees. She cites Barrymore’s authenticity and relatability as two qualities that make her a great host. “Drew authentically remembers that experience [of the commercial], and the brand means something to her,” Balzo says. “She really cares about that connection and the authenticity to the brand in this partnership, and I think people will see that come through on screen when they watch the special, which is why we’re so excited to have her as our host. [In addition], we wanted this to be about more than just baking. We want to tell the stories of a diverse set of people and their backstories and what baking means to them and memories mean to them. And she’s the perfect host to pull those stories out of our contestants. It was incredible to watch her on set because it felt like she was having just this intimate conversation with [the bakers]. I think they felt that too.”

Weintrob and showrunner Brielle Cohen watched 250 submissions from home bakers to cull the list down to 24 competitors who all have “incredible” backstories to share. In addition, famed baker and author Amirah Kassem will join Barrymore and celebrity chef judges Christina Tosi and Dook Chase in the special. It was filmed live on Oct. 23, he shares, which meant a tight turnaround for the Nov. 23 airdate.

For her part, Balzo says this was the first time General Mills had done anything “on this scale,” so they really leaned on Weintrob and the production team to guide them through the process, though GM did play a hand in everything from creative direction to final casting to set direction to the judges and host. Execs also saw all the cuts and provided feedback. (Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic is produced by Studio Large Eyes, Pantheon Media Group and Juma Entertainment. Executive producers include Weintrob for Studio Large Eyes, Jennifer O’Connell, Ariel Brozell, Eden Sutley and Martha Chaput for Pantheon, Robert Horowitz for Juma Entertainment and Brielle Cohen is showrunner. Balzo, Kenzie Caron and Eleanor Harkness serve as executive producers for Pillsbury.)

But, he adds, it’s not just matching a brand with a network and assuming the magic will happen. He says there is a lot of listening on his end and working with the brand to understand what they need while at the same time creating something that’s right for a distributor and their audience. “You’ve got to create bespoke entertainment for a brand,” he summarizes. “You can’t just send them random ideas.”

There’s also the challenge of the promotional timeline for brands vs. distributors. Brands usually begin working on their promotional campaigns months out, while the distributors work on a shorter timeline, sometimes even just weeks. Weintrob says he worked with both companies to come up with an approach that benefited each of them.

Both Weintrob and Balzo hope this special becomes an annual tradition that families can enjoy for years. And, Weintrob suggests, the special could expand to include Valentine’s Day or Super Bowl editions, for example.

“As a brand and especially the Pillsbury brand, the whole family is so important,” Balzo adds. “So we wanted to make sure that we created something that could be one of those moments to bring families together around and create memories around.”

Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic airs Nov. 23 from 8-10 p.m. ET/PT on CBS and streams on Paramount+ (Premium).

Voyager 1 should keep running until at least its 50th anniversary next year. What happens next is up to physics — and chance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.

Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s.

Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space?

Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018.

"Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email.

Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email.

"Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question."

The team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers launched, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is.

Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Big Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science.

Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1).

A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space.

"Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did quickly recover.

"The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause."

Voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

"They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin said in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather important details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of issues.

"One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he said the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it."

While there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team says it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said.

Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again."

Editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#661. Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

Events were held for "Volkstrauertag," a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts said the country is headed for a budget crisis.

This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he said.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police launched a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in."

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

The bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk."

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Police said there had been some clashes with participants.   A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

#660. Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world."

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result

In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

By using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope."

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings

Achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin."

In other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve

The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open new possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

For now, one of the most important outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out."

Materials provided by Delft University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#659. How Iran’s Pegah Ahangarani Turned Her Family Archives Into a Regime-Challenging Oscar Hopeful

The director of 'Rehearsals for a Revolution,' the U.K.'s submission for best international feature at the Academy Awards, on 40 years of Iranian history told through her own life — and how an exile built the film with almost no money.

“Cinema is not just part of my life,” begins Pegah Ahangarani. “It’s me, actually.”

The director and actress grew up on film sets. Both of her parents were filmmakers themselves and immersed their children in the Iranian entertainment industry. Ahangarani became a child star, skyrocketing to fame at just 14 in 1999’s The Girl in the Sneakers. “I won a lot of awards,” she smiles to The Hollywood Reporter. But even she couldn’t have predicted the award-winning success of her debut feature-length documentary, Rehearsals for a Revolution. Related Stories Movies Record Number of International and Animated Features Oscar-Eligible This Season Music Don Toliver Postpones O2 Arena Show After Evacuation Due to "Unknown Substance" Released at Manchester Concert

The Cannes-premiering — and L’Œil d’or-winning — project is a poignant reminder of the power of memory. Ahangarani, whose other essay documentaries include shorts I Am Trying to Remember (2021), My Father (2023) and Child Soldier (2024), sketches her entire life story in this latest work. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s turbulent history. From the late ’70s up until the war with the U.S. and Israel, Ahangarani pieces together and narrates intimate recollections from her life — the vanilla scent of her schoolteacher’s hair and desperate search for her uncle in videos from the 1999 Iranian student protests among them — that help to form the portrait of a country shaped by political repression, and in constant hope for a revolution.

Personal is the operative word in this co-production between the Czech Republic and Spain. “I want to tell my audience: ‘Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility,'” says its director. As daunting as that task was — Ahangarani has already been arrested and spent time in the notorious Evin Prison, and expects not to be able to return to Iran at the risk of a lengthy jail sentence following the release of this film — she remains steadfast in her belief that using family archives is the greatest weapon at her disposal against the regime. “I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'” says Ahangarani. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.”

Having left Iran in 2022, Ahangarani shares candid reflections with viewers about the guilt she’s experienced in the wake of this year’s civilian massacres and brutal crackdown on the Woman, Life, Freedom movement back home. From London, where she has been settled since 2023, Ahangarani talks to THR about putting that guilt up on screen — and being selected as the U.K.’s submission for best international feature film at the 2027 Oscars: “When you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land… [Now], there is one place that accepted me.”

You grew up in film and TV. You were a child star. But when did you first realize you’d like to direct films yourself?

I grew up in cinema, yes. All of the crew members were like my family members. I called them aunties and uncles. (Laughs.) I cannot separate myself from cinema. Cinema is not just part of my life — it’s me, actually. I started cinema as my main career when I was 14. I acted in one film, The Girl in the Sneakers, and that film became very successful. I won a lot of awards. I was a teenager, and I was super happy. And then a few years after that, I remember I saw some documentaries and I thought, “OK, I’d like to maybe be a documentary filmmaker.” I made a few documentaries, but they were very naive. It [was] TV-style documentaries. Then I got familiar with [the] essay style in literature, and then I started exploring that style in some documentaries. I saw some Chris Marker documentaries for example, and Jonas Mekas.

I thought maybe I should find that style for myself, so six or seven years ago I made a short documentary with this style. I used personal archives and I used my voiceover as a narration, and I started making very personal documentaries. That film became very successful as well. The New Yorker published that documentary. It premiered at IDFA Film Festival and a lot of festivals after that. And then I made another short documentary, same style, and another one again. And then after those three documentaries, I started making this one.

The archive of film and photos you use in this is just incredible. Is it daunting, or were you nervous, crafting an entire project around such intimate artefacts and stories?

Yes, actually. (Laughs.) I had a lot of concern about it, and not just for this film. […] A few years ago, when I was living in Iran, I went to my grandmother’s house, and I found some old family albums there. And I started looking through the photographs, and then I saw one photo. My mom was there. My father was there. I was there too. I was two or three years old, and I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. And I asked my grandmother, “Who is this person? Why has his face been scratched out?” She said, “He was your father’s best friend. He was executed after the revolution because he was a political prisoner.” And I realized my grandmother didn’t destroy the whole photo. She kept that photo, just scratched that face. After that shocking moment, I realized that maybe my responsibility as a documentary filmmaker is to find these old family photos, this personal footage, and find these scratched-out faces and bring them back to life, bring them back to the frame, and bring them back to our collective memory.

After that, I thought a lot about these archives, and I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools.’ Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe. From that day, I started thinking about how I should use these materials as my facts. […] If you go deeper [into] one photograph, if you focus on it, you can see the part of our history in that photograph. But that wasn’t easy at all. When I made that short documentary, I sent it to my mother because my mother was one of the characters, my father was one of the characters, and I had a lot of concern because they might be in trouble after that film. But they were okay. I remember one thing: I sent my film to my grandmother, and I told her, “Okay, I made a short documentary based on the photo that you kept for me.” And she said, “Yes, maybe I kept that photo just for you to make this documentary.”

This is a co-production between Spain and the Czech Republic, is that right? What work went into getting this over the line? Because using your own photos, films and narration, it strikes me as incredibly inexpensive documentary.

[It was made] with nothing, actually. (Laughs.) I had a producer [with whom] I made three of my short documentaries, Kaveh Farnam [founder of the Czech Republic’s Media Nest], and he’s an Iranian independent film [producer] outside of Iran. I remember when I was making a previous documentary, I found him, I texted him, and he joined the project. And that one was like this — I didn’t need money because I worked with my personal archives. But I wanted support for distribution [and] things. At that time, I was inside Iran, and I told Mr. Farnum that after this film, if I got arrested or something like that, please publish the film. I needed someone just for publishing. And then when I moved to London, I talked to Mr. Farnum about this feature film, and he said, “Okay, I’m in,” and I didn’t need any money for that. I just needed a small [amount of] money for my editor [Arash Ashtiani]. The Spain company [Fasten Films]… they found me and they wanted me to make another film for them. And then I told them, “I have one film, it’s finished now. I can send it to you, and if you want, you can join this project as well.” Right after they watched the film, they texted me and they told me, “Oh, we love the film. We want to join the project.”

They supported us because we needed some money for the copyright of the music and sound design, and they have a good relationship with a French distributor… Then they sent the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and they have a very good relationship with Cannes because they are French, and everything actually happened after that. But for the process of making this, we didn’t need any money.

One standout part of the documentary, for me, is when you’re scrolling through some of those harrowing images and videos from this year’s protests and you talk about your guilt and trying to compensate for that with the film. What has it been like reckoning with that through these glamorous film festivals?

Everything was very strange because right after the massacre, we were in the process of editing episode five. We wanted to show me [and] my new life as an immigrant, living in exile, and then war happened and massacre happened, and so we didn’t know how we should respond [to] these disasters in our film. That was a very complicated situation because I couldn’t focus on the film. I told my editor, “Cinema doesn’t mean [anything] anymore after all these dead bodies.” And then I realized that, “Okay, I should share all these concerns with my audience because this is the only way I should tell them.”

But I didn’t have any idea that the the film [could] be successful. During the process of making this, it was just me and my editor, Arash, and a little mic, and a very intimate space. I remember the distribution company texted me and told me the director of Cannes, Thierry Frémaux, told us maybe you can be in the official selection. That was very exciting. That day, I just lay down on the sofa in our office… I couldn’t handle this much excitement. We realized we can compete with, for example, Steven Soderbergh, because he had a film in Cannes in the official documentary selection. And in Cannes, they told us, “You won the best documentary prize,” and I think I’m in the middle of some dream or something like that. Not because my film is successful now, but because I try to show these 40 years of Iranian history and this ongoing struggle of the Iranian people, and everybody around the world now can see this struggle.

What do you hope audiences are talking and thinking about after seeing this film?

After the first screening in Cannes, I realized one thing, which was very sweet: When the film finished and people started clapping, many of them came and told me, “We think we love your people as much as you.” I thought, ‘So this is cinema.’ You can show something that people don’t have any idea about, and they can resonate with it, and they can feel this struggle. They can feel [for] your people, which is amazing.

Many people, after watching the film, they think they know me very well [and that] they’re a friend of mine, which is very sweet. I think the film is successful because I could create a sense of intimacy. Through the narration and through the film, I want to tell my audience: “Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility.”

This film is officially the U.K.’s official Oscar submission for best international feature. What does that mean to you?

That was great news. Not just because of the film, but when you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land. When I left Iran, I thought, “OK, this is just a temporary situation.” And then I realized that no, maybe it’s permanent. I cannot go back anymore. I should accept my new life, and that was very difficult. When the U.K. announced that they picked our film … I had a feeling like I wasn’t stateless anymore. There is one place that accepted me.

I’m sure you miss your family so much, but you don’t envision a future where you can return?

When I left Iran in 2021, I didn’t have any plan to stay outside of Iran. I left my country with just one carry-on to participate in the IDFA Film Festival for my short documentary. And after the second screening, my mother, she was in Iran [and] called me and told me the regime had called her and asked her to interrogate me about the film. She told me, “Stay outside for a while, for one or two months.” And then the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement happened and I published a video to show my solidarity with that movement, and then my mother told me they sent a letter [saying] there is a court order against me. They seized my apartment and my bank accounts in Iran and I realized that I can’t go back. If I go back, I have to go to jail. I was in jail for one month in solitary [confinement], but if I go back, maybe I could be in jail for six or seven years or something like that. I decided to stay outside because I wanted to make my film.

Common Space has chosen Satellogic to build and operate its first high-resolution Earth-observing spacecraft.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan.

The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.

That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites: Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company.

There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery.

Satellogic is now officially part of this picture.

"With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come."

The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process.

The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth. But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm).

The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully.

And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed.

"Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice."

Common Space is currently raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit.

Editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

#657. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease."

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," said Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see."

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

The results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies."

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," said Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies."

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," said Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment."

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal new treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

#656. Amanda Seyfried, Robert De Niro and Timothee Chalamet to Host ‘SNL’ in December

Here are all of season 52's hosts and musical guests.

After leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in more than half a century, Jalen Brunson will add another accomplishment to his career highlights this fall: Saturday Night Live host.

Brunson is set to host the Sept. 26 season premiere of SNL and will be joined by musical guest KATSEYE. He’s the first athlete to host the show in more than three years (Travis Kelce was the most recent one, in March 2023) and the first active NBA player to take center stage at studio 8H since LeBron James back in 2007.

Dakota Johnson (Oct. 3) and Shane Gillis (Oct. 10) will each host SNL for the third time in the fall. Johnson will be joined musical guest Turnstile, and Rosalia will be the musical guest for Gillis’ episode. SNL then takes a couple weeks off before returning on Halloween with Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette making her debut as host and musical guest Gracie Abrams. Related Stories TV NBC to Air Princess of Wales Cancer Charity Documentary TV 'The Traitors: New Blood' Renewed for Second Season at NBC

On Nov. 7, comedian and online/social media creator Druski will make his hosting debut (his booking was first reported at Puck). He’s the first person to make the leap from the online creator world to hosting SNL, though Druski has also had several TV, movie and commercial roles and hosted the BET Awards in June. The Strokes will be the musical guest for the episode, the band’s fifth time on the show.

A week later, comedian and former SNL writer John Mulaney will host for the seventh time. Phoebe Bridgers will make her second appearance as musical guest.

The show will close out 2026 with three shows. Amanda Seyfried will host on Dec. 5 with musical guest Don Toliver; it will be the first time for both. On Dec. 12, Robert De Niro hosts for the fourth time, with Slayyyter debuting as the musical guest. Timothee Chalamet hosts the Christmas show on Dec. 19 (also his fourth time), and Charli xcx will make her fourth appearance as the musical guest.

The cast of SNL will be fairly stable — at least compared to the sizable overhaul prior to season 51 last year. Chloe Fineman announced her departure from the show in July after seven seasons, and writer and occasional performer Martin Herlihy left after five seasons. The rest of last season’s cast, however, is returning, and Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter are joining the show as featured players.

The full list of hosts and musical guests for season 52 of SNL is below. This story will be updated as more shows are announced.

Sept. 26: Jalen Brunson, KATSEYEOct. 3: Dakota Johnson, TurnstileOct. 10: Shane Gillis, RosaliaOct. 31: Inde Navarrette, Gracie AbramsNov. 7: Druski, The StrokesNov. 14: John Mulaney, Phoebe BridgersDec. 5: Amanda Seyfried, Don ToliverDec. 12: Robert De Niro, SlayyyterDec. 19: Timothee Chalamet, Charli xcx

From colorful meteors to lingering trails, the Leonids put on a great show this year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows."

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this. -- November 18, 2026 York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3November 18, 2026

This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, New Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

"But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog."

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

"One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

#654. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

#653. Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies."

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research

The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur."

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

Materials provided by University of Waterloo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
